arguments.conclusion: Higher levels of government debt and money supply today than in 1960-1980 change the effect of interest rate changes on inflation.

arguments.premise_synthesis: The argument rests on two key structural differences between the present and the 1960-1980 period. First, U.S. government debt-to-GDP has risen from around 30% in that earlier era to over 100% and near 125% today. Second, the money supply relative to the size of the economy is much larger now than at least since 1980. These differences imply that the economic impact of interest rate changes—including their effect on inflation—is no longer the same as historically observed.
arguments.conclusion_supported: The argument supports the broader claim that the Federal Reserve's monetary policy framework is fundamentally flawed because the conventional inverse relationship between interest rates and inflation is inverted or altered by high debt and money supply levels, contributing to the inevitability of a sovereign debt crisis.
